results.content: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning algorithms implementations. 476 stars 89 forks Branches Tags Activity. # LucasAlegre/morl-baselines. # MORL-Baselines. MORL-Baselines is a library of Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning (MORL) algorithms. This repository aims to contain reliable MORL algorithms implementations in PyTorch. For details on multi-objective MDPs (MOMDPs) and other MORL definitions, we suggest reading A practical guide to multi-objective reinforcement learning and planning. An overview of some techniques used in various MORL algorithms is also provided in Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning Based on Decomposition: A Taxonomy and Framework. A tutorial on MO-Gymnasium and MORL-Baselines is also available:. * Single and multi-policy algorithms under both SER and ESR criteria are implemented. * All algorithms follow the MO-Gymnasium API. * All algorithms are automatically tested. ## Implemented Algorithms. MORL-Baselines participates to Open RL Benchmark which contains tracked experiments from popular RL libraries such as cleanRL and Stable Baselines 3. We have run experiments of our algorithms on various environments from MO-Gymnasium. As much as possible, this repo tries to follow the single-file implementation rule for all algorithms. * `examples/` contains a set of examples to use MORL Baselines with MO-Gymnasium environments. * `multi_policy/` contains the implementations of multi-policy algorithms. * `single_policy/` contains the implementations of single-policy algorithms (ESR and SER). If you use MORL-Baselines in your research, please cite our NeurIPS 2023 paper:. C. and Talbi, El Ghazali and Danoy, Gr{\'e}goire and Silva, Bruno Castro da}{} title{A Toolkit for Reliable Benchmarking and Research in Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning}{} booktitle{Proceedings of the 37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems ({NeurIPS} 2023)}{} year{2023}{}. MORL-Baselines is currently maintained by Florian Felten (@ffelten) and Lucas N. This repository is open to contributions and we are always happy to receive new algorithms, bug fixes, or features. * Willem Röpke (@wilrop), for his original implementation of IPRO(-2D) and reimplementation of non-linear MO-PPO and Pareto Q-Learning. * Mathieu Reymond, for providing us with the original implementation of PCN. Hayes, for providing us with the original implementation of EUPG. * Jayden Teoh, for providing several improvements in different algorithms and the implementation of MOSAC discrete. results.title: Benchmarking Multi-agent Deep Reinforcement Learning Algorithms
results.content: To investigate the consistency of the performance of MARL algorithms, we build an open-source library of multi-agent algorithms including DDPG/TD3/SAC with centralized Q functions, PPO with centralized value functions, as well as QMix, and test them across a range of tasks that vary in coordination difficulty and agent number. QMix (Rashid et al., 2018) is a Q-learning algorithm designed for multi-agent cooperative. In addition to partial observability, in our benchmark analysis we consider and study the following assumptions of interest: (a) we utilize the celebrated CTDE MARL schema [32], which has been widely adopted by the cooperative MARL community [2,16] as it enables conditioning approximate value functions on privileged information in a computationally tractable manner, (b) we evaluate fully cooperative tasks, that is, tasks where there are no adversarial non-learnable agents (e.g., bots), or teams of opponent agents, interacting with the learnable agents, (c) we also evaluate complex tasks with sparse-reward settings that require excessive joint exploration and cooperation to be solved, (d) we also study tasks with image-based, high-dimensional state and observation spaces (as in real-world tasks), which have been very frequent in single-agent RL but not in MARL evaluation, and (e) as in [36,63] we assume that agents lack explicit communication channels during execution. Next, we test the performance of the proposed FMASAC algorithm in the scenario with three UAVs and three targets and compare it with three baselines: the MASAC [39], multiagent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) [40], and multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG) [22] algorithms. We extend three classes of single-agent deep reinforcement learning algorithms based on policy gradient, temporal-difference error, and actor-critic methods to cooperative multi-agent systems. We show that policy gradient methods tend to outperform both temporal-difference and actor-critic methods and that curriculum learning is vital to scaling reinforcement learning algorithms in complex multi-agent domains. [Show full abstract]]() state-of-the-art in three popular multi-agent testbeds: the Particle World environments, Starcraft II Micromanagement Tasks, and the Hanabi Challenge, with minimal hyperparameter tuning and without any domain-specific algorithmic modifications or architectures. It almost reaches a consensus that off-policy algorithms dominated research benchmarks of multi-agent reinforcement learning, while recent work [34] demonstrates that on-policy MARL algorithm, Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO), can also attain comparable performance.

results.title: Learning Fair Pareto-Optimal Policies in Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning | OpenReview
results.content: Go to **AAMAS 2025 Workshop ALA** homepage. ## Learning Fair Pareto-Optimal Policies in Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning. ### Umer Siddique, Peilang Li, Yongcan Cao. Published: 01 Apr 2025, Last Modified: 02 May 2025ALAEveryoneRevisionsBibTeXCC BY 4.0. **Keywords:** Multi-objective reinforcement learning, Deep reinforcement learning, Fair optimization, Welfare functions. **Abstract:** Fairness is an important aspect of decision-making in multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL), where policies must ensure both optimality and equity across multiple, potentially conflicting objectives. While $single-policy$ MORL methods can learn fair policies for fixed user preferences using welfare functions such as the generalized Gini welfare function (GGF), they fail to provide the diverse set of policies necessary for dynamic or unknown user preferences. To address this limitation, we formalize the fair optimization problem in $multi-policy$ MORL, where the goal is to learn a set of Pareto-optimal policies that ensure fairness across all possible user preferences. Our key technical contributions are threefold: (1) We show that for concave, piecewise-linear welfare functions (e.g., GGF), fair policies remain in the convex coverage set (CCS), which is an approximated Pareto front for linear scalarization. (2) We demonstrate that non-stationary policies, augmented with accrued reward histories, and stochastic policies improve fairness by dynamically adapting to historical inequities. (3) We propose three novel algorithms, which include integrating GGF with multi-policy multi-objective Q-Learning (MOQL), state-augmented multi-policy MOQL for learning non-statoinary policies, and its novel extension for learning stochastic policies. To validate the performance of the proposed algorithms, we perform experiments in various domains and compare our methods against the state-of-the-art MORL baselines. The empirical results show that our methods learn a set of fair policies that accommodate different user preferences. **Type Of Paper:** Full paper (max page 8). results.title: Day 93/100: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning – Balancing Competing Goals | by Sebastian Buzdugan | Medium
results.content: # Day 93/100: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning – Balancing Competing Goals. Welcome to the nuanced world of Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning (MORL). ## 🎯 Why Multi-Objective RL? • A self-driving car must maximize speed while minimizing risk. • A recommender system should increase engagement without promoting harmful content. Multi-Objective RL acknowledges these trade-offs:. Train agents that can balance and negotiate between competing objectives. ## 🔎 What Is Multi-Objective RL? Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning (MORL) involves optimizing multiple reward signals, each representing a different objective. • A solution is Pareto optimal if improving one objective worsens at least one other. • The set of all such solutions forms the Pareto front. • Convert multiple objectives into a single reward using a weighted sum. • Simple and fast, but the weights need careful tuning. • Learn policies conditioned on user or system-defined preferences over objectives. • Can dynamically adapt based on context or changing priorities. • Train multiple policies, each specializing in a different region of the Pareto front. • Useful when a single unified policy isn’t feasible. • Fixed or learnable weights to combine objectives. • Works well when trade-offs are linear. • Learns a set of Pareto-efficient Q-functions. • Explores policies that cannot be dominated. • Condition the policy on a preference vector. • One model handles many trade-off configurations. • Assign agents to different objectives. • Use coordination strategies to resolve conflicts. • Gym-MORL: Environments supporting multi-objective formulations. • MOMDP Benchmarks: Multi-objective MDPs for testing policies. • PyMORL / MORL-Baselines: Open-source implementations of scalarization, Pareto RL, etc. • Ray RLlib: Can be extended to multi-reward tasks via custom envs. • Metarl / Garage: Good for research in multi-policy and preference-based methods. • Understand the objective conflicts in your domain. • Experiment with different scalarization methods. • Use preference queries to guide trade-offs. • Evaluate using coverage of the Pareto front, not just scalar rewards. • Incorporate user feedback to align trade-offs with human expectations. • Weight tuning is non-trivial and domain-dependent. • High-dimensional Pareto fronts are hard to explore and interpret. • Policy generalization across objectives is difficult. • Sparse feedback per objective can slow convergence. • Balancing objectives may require dynamic re-weighting.

Call the `train` method for training iterations # Example pseudocode reward_dim = env.reward_space.shape[0] # Create network network = MOPPONet(obs_shape, action_shape, reward_dim, net_arch=[64, 64]) # Create weights for scalarization weights = np.array([0.5, 0.5]) # For 2 objectives # Create MOPPO policy # Training loop for i in range(max_iterations): policy.train(start_time, i, max_iterations) Sources: morl_baselines/single_policy/ser/mo_ppo.py 580-613 MOPPO inherits evaluation methods from the `MOPolicy` base class: * `policy_eval`: Evaluates the policy by running multiple episodes and computing average returns * `policy_eval_esr`: Evaluates the policy using Expected Scalarized Return Both methods support logging to Weights & Biases for tracking performance.
